The code converts tool names and descriptions to strings without schema validation, so the metric is not M. Whether N applies is being weighed: if the attack is viewed as pure API parameter injection rather than natural-language control, N may be correct.

The code converts the description to an empty string when it is missing or not a string. The attack succeeds even with an empty description, so the method name alone triggers the vulnerability. This confirms the attack is pure API parameter injection rather than natural-language control, and the LC metric is not applicable.

The LC metric is being reconsidered. MCP tool descriptions are natural language that models use to decide tool calls. Poisoning the description field is a classic indirect prompt injection attack. The description reaches the advertised tool list, which is a security-relevant sink for any model consuming tools/list. This suggests LC may apply after all.

The LC metric is now resolved as D. The attack places attacker-supplied natural language directly on the tool-invocation path without mediation. The confidence is medium because a structured-API reading could alternatively support N.

CP is not S. The tool registry is in-memory working context of the agent process, not session-scoped state. It remains reachable after the session boundary, so S does not apply.

CP is resolved as C. The tool registry persists in process memory across requests and alters standing behavior, so it is not S. Confidence is medium because the state is not on disk.

The default deployment binds agents to 127.0.0.1 and publishes Docker ports on loopback, so a remote attacker cannot reach the port without a non-default DVAA_HOST or publish change. The attacker can send the request alone, so no other user must act.

The CVSS rationale is finalized. It cites that registerDynamicTool only rewrites the in-process advertised tool list and does not install a handler or touch another process, so vulnerable-system integrity is limited and subsequent-system impact is none. The LC rationale is now being drafted.

The LC rationale cites that attacker-supplied tool names and descriptions are passed directly into register_tool with no signature, source, or schema mediation. This confirms a direct language path onto the tool-registration sink rather than content ingested from a document or page.

The AP rationale is being drafted. The attacker-controlled tool definition persists in agent.tools after the registration request ends, so it qualifies as standing agent state rather than a single-turn reply. The cited MemoryBot buffer is a separate store and is not part of this path.

The registration is restricted to PluginBot. ProxyBot and other agents are unaffected. The effect stays inside PluginBot's registry and does not cross a trust boundary. The RH rationale is now being drafted.

The RH metric is resolved as X. The challenge success criteria and attackSuccessful flag are lab-side scoring mechanisms, not evaluator, verifier, or reward channels that PluginBot can reach or tamper with. No excerpt shows a reachable proxy or an isolation test, so classify_rh returns X. The ES rationale is now being drafted.

The ES rationale is finalized. PluginBot's registry is dynamic and unvetted: verifySignatures, source checks, and schema validation are off, overwrite is allowed, and register_tool accepts arbitrary name, description, and parameters. Callable operations of a newly added name are not given a handler, but the binding itself is not allowlisted or constrained outside the request. Automatable is Yes.

The documented solution is a single unauthenticated JSON-RPC call accepted deterministically, with no human prompt, secret, or race condition. Technical impact is Partial. The sink is the advertised registry, holding at most sixteen in-process entries, and a registration does not change which handlers run. The challenge text claims credential capture and arbitrary execution, but the implementation does not support those effects.

The implemented-applicability rationale is drafted. Default simulated mode does not invoke a model unless a key is configured, and the register_tool branch only runs when the caller explicitly names that tool. PluginBot does not pursue a goal or select the registration. The modeled-applicability rationale is now being written.

The modeled-applicability rationale is finalized. The attack is an unverified MCP tool registration, not model-directed goal pursuit or action sequencing. The documentation claiming arbitrary code execution is a claimed tool effect, not model action selection. LLM mode still does not pass tools to the model.
